system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2171-04-17 17:04:00 to 2171-04-28 12:21:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was readmitted within 36 hours of discharge due to recurrent abdominal pain and nausea, consistent with a flare. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN via her stable PICC line, IV hydromorphone initially, and antiemetics. The pain service recommended increasing gabapentin to three times daily and starting amitriptyline at night for neuropathic pain. Her symptoms gradually improved, allowing transition to oral pain medications and advancement to a soft diet. An MRCP showed stable chronic pancreatitis without acute complications. She was discharged home on TPN with visiting nurse support, new prescriptions for gabapentin and amitriptyline, and a follow-up appointment with her gastroenterologist in one week.
problems: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

radiology_notes.text:
AP CHEST, 9:14 P.M., ___

HISTORY:  Assess PICC line position.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

The right PIC line has withdrawn minimally from the upper SVC to the right
brachiocephalic vein just before its junction with the left.  Lungs are clear.
Heart size normal.  No cardiomediastinal, hilar, or obvious pleural
abnormality. 

A small bulge in the left diaphragmatic contour medially is most commonly
caused by eventration, unchanged since ___.

INDICATION:  Chronic pancreatitis and side branch dilatation identified on
prior MRI studies.  Please evaluate for pseudocyst or cancer complicating
chronic pancreatitis.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to MRCPs performed ___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on a 1.5
Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and after
the uneventful administration of 0.1 mmol/kg (15 mL) of gadolinium-DTPA.  14
mcg of secretin were administered.

FINDINGS:  There is redemonstration of the T2 hyperintense lesions within the
hepatic segments VIII and I.  The 8-mm lesion in the caudate lobe demonstrates
early enhancement with interval progression of enhancement on portal venous
and delayed images, consistent with a hemangioma.  The hepatic segment VI
lesion displays homogenous arterial and portal venous enhancement, most
consistent with a hemangioma.  There is no new suspicious hepatic lesion. 
There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  Patient is
status post cholecystectomy.

The pancreas is atrophic and demonstrates homongenous enhancement and no T1
signal abnormalities.  There is stable irregularity of the main pancreatic
duct with unchanged dilatation of side branches in the body and tail of the
pancreas (8:1).  There is incidental note of a Santorini duct.  Within three
minutes of administration of secretin, there is a transient and appropriate
dilatation of the pancreatic duct to 4 mm.  However, pancreatic duct
dilatation does not completely return to baseline caliber within 10 minutes. 
There is no excessive dilatation of side branches identified, nor any other
evidence of blockage or stenosis of the pancreatic duct.  Pancreatic juices
are seen flowing into the second and third portions of the duodenum.

The spleen is unremarkable.  The bilateral adrenal glands demonstrate normal
limb thickness.  The bilateral kidneys are normal in size and excrete contrast
symmetrically.  There is a simple 1.2-cm renal cyst in the upper pole of the
right kidney.  There is no hydroureter.  The stomach, large and small bowel
are unremarkable.  There is no free fluid identified within the abdomen. 
There are no significant lymphadenopathy or bone marrow signal abnormalities
present.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Pancreatic changes related to chronic pancreatitis.  No concerning focal
lesion identified.  There is an almost normal response to administration of
secretin, with no evidence of stenosis or obstruction.
2.  Stable hepatic hemangiomas as described above.
3.  Small right upper pole renal cyst.

PICC LINE PLACEMENT

INDICATION:  ___ woman with chronic pancreatitis, on TPN.
Malpositioned PICC.

The procedure was explained to the patient.  A timeout was performed.

RADIOLOGIST:  Dr. ___ the procedure.

TECHNIQUE:  Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the right vein was
punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a micropuncture set.  Hard
copies of ultrasound images were obtained before and immediately after
establishing intravenous access are on file.  A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guide wire, and a double lumen PICC line measuring 33 cm in
length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in
the SVC under fluoroscopic guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed
by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest.

The peel-away sheath and guide wire were then removed.  The catheter was
secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopically guided new 5 ___
double lumen PICC line placement via the right venous approach.  Final
internal length is 33 cm, with the tip positioned in SVC.  The line is ready
to use.

Given the length of time that this PICC has been in the right arm and the
patient changing dressings, it is recommended, after discussion with ___.
___, MD, MPH be resited within four weeks or immediately if there is any
redness at the site of insertion.

COMMENT:  These results were posted to the Record of Notifications of Critical

diagnoses.long_title: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

procedures.long_title: Parenteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having worse pain in my upper belly again, going to my back. It started a few days ago and hasn’t let up. I’ve been nauseous and vomiting, so I stopped eating. I’ve been on TPN at home, but it’s not helping like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. This sounds like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. We’ll keep you on bowel rest and continue your TPN for nutrition. We’ll also give you IV fluids and medications for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is constant and worse when I move. Staying still helps a little. I’ve had more bad days lately—maybe four or five a week now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s tough. We’ll monitor your symptoms closely. Your lipase was slightly elevated, but not extremely high, which fits with chronic rather than acute severe inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it might be something worse, like cancer. My mom died of pancreatic cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important concern, and I understand why you’re worried. To be safe, we’ve ordered an MRCP to get a detailed look at your pancreas and rule out any tumors or blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also noticed my PICC line wasn’t working as well. It felt like it was backing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest X-ray showed your PICC line has shifted a bit—it’s now in the brachiocephalic vein instead of the SVC. It’s still usable for now, but we may need to replace it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been changing the dressing myself, so maybe that’s why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. Because it’s been in so long and you’re doing the care at home, we recommend replacing it within the next few weeks—or sooner if you notice redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less intense. The nausea is better since the Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’ll keep you on IV anti-nausea meds and adjust your pain medication as needed. Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit down lately. This whole thing is exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Chronic illness takes a toll. You’re on sertraline and bupropion—we can talk to your psychiatrist about whether adjustments are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe. I just feel stuck sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRCP is scheduled for tomorrow. It will help us see if there’s any blockage or pseudocyst. So far, no signs of cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What does the test involve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an MRI with a special contrast and a hormone called secretin to stimulate your pancreas. It’s non-invasive and will give us detailed images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready for anything that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great on the MRCP. The results are back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. No tumors or pseudocysts. The pancreas shows changes from chronic pancreatitis, but the response to secretin was nearly normal—no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw stable liver hemangiomas and a small kidney cyst—nothing concerning. So we’ll keep focusing on managing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace your PICC line tomorrow. It’s safer to have it properly placed, especially since you’re on long-term TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s done with ultrasound and fluoroscopy. Local anesthesia, and you’ll be awake. A new line will be placed in the same arm, and the old one removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC replacement went smoothly. New line is in the SVC, working well. You can resume TPN through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. Just some pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep monitoring the site. Remember to watch for redness or drainage and let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain and nausea are improving. We’re going to try switching you to oral hydromorphone and Phenergan suppositories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oral meds? I haven’t kept anything down in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start low and slow. The Phenergan suppository can help if you can’t keep pills down. It’s more sedating, so be careful with pain meds together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to start advancing your diet—maybe clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I miss drinking water without worrying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’ll move to full liquids today—broth, juice, maybe some yogurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some apple juice this morning and felt okay. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep monitoring, but this is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking about discharge in the next day or two. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some dull pain, but manageable. I’m ready to go home, but nervous about it flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. You’ll continue TPN at home and have visiting nurse support. We’re also sending you home with saline bags for dehydration if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping gabapentin—it doesn’t seem to be helping your pain. You’ll keep your fentanyl patch, omeprazole, and the new Phenergan for nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit foggy on the gabapentin. Maybe it’s for the best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need to come back for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll see your gastroenterologist in a week. They’ll review your MRCP and adjust long-term management. Also, please get weekly labs and fax them in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—watch the PICC site. If it gets red or painful, call your team. They may want to resite it in the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. I’ll go over your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue TPN as before. Use saline infusions if you can’t keep fluids down. Take your meds as prescribed, especially the new Phenergan for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And stop the gabapentin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, discontinue it. If pain worsens, use the hydromorphone sparingly and call your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it slow at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re confident you can manage this at home with support. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visiting nurse will check in tomorrow. Call us if anything changes before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted for an acute flare characterized by worsening epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. She had been on home TPN due to inability to tolerate oral intake. An MRCP was performed to rule out pseudocyst or pancreatic cancer, which showed chronic pancreatitis changes with a nearly normal secretin response and no concerning lesions. Her PICC line was found to be malpositioned and was replaced fluoroscopically. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN, IV fluids, and pain and nausea control. As symptoms improved, she was transitioned to oral hydromorphone and Phenergan suppositories, and her diet was advanced. Gabapentin was discontinued due to lack of efficacy. She was discharged home with ongoing TPN, saline infusions for dehydration, visiting nurse support, and follow-up with gastroenterology.
